# Pointwise is not uniform

## Beat 1 — Who chooses the threshold?

Content needed: Begin with the two definitions on a domain D: pointwise, for every x in D and every epsilon > 0, there exists N such that all n >= N satisfy |f_n(x)-f(x)| < epsilon; uniform, for every epsilon > 0, there exists N such that every x in D and every n >= N satisfy the same inequality. Mark N=N(x,epsilon) versus N=N(epsilon). Use identical error notation and distinguish the order of the quantifiers.

Narration: Pointwise convergence means this: for every point x and every positive tolerance epsilon, there is a threshold N after which the difference between f n of x and f of x is smaller than epsilon. The threshold may depend on the point as well as the tolerance.

Narration: Uniform convergence changes the order. For every positive epsilon, there is one threshold N that works for every point x, for all indices beyond that threshold. We choose the tolerance, then the threshold, before knowing which point will be tested. Both definitions demand that every later index works. The difference is whether different points can need different thresholds.

## Beat 2 — Find the limit, including the endpoint

Content needed: On D=[0,1], f_n(x)=x^n for integer n>=1. Graph selected powers n=1,2,8,32 with fixed axes, then retain one current curve. Pointwise limit f(x)=0 for 0<=x<1 and f(1)=1. The limit graph has an open marker at (1,0) and filled marker at (1,1). Error e_n(x)=|f_n(x)-f(x)| is x^n below 1 but is 0 at 1. Introduce error only after establishing the limit.

Narration: Consider x to the power n on the closed interval from zero to one. At any fixed point strictly between zero and one, repeated multiplication by that same number drives the value to zero. At zero, every value is already zero. At one, however, every value is one.

Narration: So the pointwise limit is zero below one, and one at the endpoint. Keep that endpoint: we are not comparing our functions with the zero function everywhere. Below one, the error is x to the power n. At one, the error is zero, because the function and its limit both equal one. As n grows, the graph drops near each fixed interior point. Does that give a common threshold?

## Beat 3 — Let the test point move

Content needed: Initially show the current power curve and established limit only. Pose the prediction for epsilon=1/4 without a witness, half-height guide, answer label, or highlighted near-endpoint region during the pause. At Reveal introduce x_n=2^(-1/n), with 0<x_n<1 and x_n^n=1/2. For increasing n, calculate the witness and curve from the same exponent; the witness approaches 1 from below while its error remains 1/2. Show e_n(1)=0 separately. State sup_{x in [0,1]} e_n(x)=1, not attained, only after the witness argument.

Invitation (spoken): Set the tolerance to one quarter. Could some index make the error smaller than this at every point? Take a few seconds to decide, remembering that the test point can depend on the index.

Pause: 5s

Reveal (spoken): No. For any positive index n, choose x to be the nth root of one half. This point lies strictly below one, so its limiting value is zero. But its nth power is exactly one half. Its error therefore exceeds one quarter, however large n is.

Narration: These are different test points, moving toward one. Pointwise convergence holds each point fixed; uniform convergence must also withstand this moving choice. In fact, for each n, errors approach one as x approaches one from below. Their supremum is one, although the error at one itself is zero.

## Beat 4 — A boundary away from one

Content needed: Restrict the same family to [0,a], with fixed 0<a<1. Mark the excluded interval (a,1] before removing it from the active domain. Use a=0.8 only as an illustrative drawing; label the argument for general fixed a. The restricted pointwise limit is identically zero. For every x in [0,a], 0<=x^n<=a^n, so sup_{x in [0,a]}|f_n(x)-0|=a^n -> 0, attained at x=a. For any epsilon>0 choose N with a^N<epsilon; all n>=N have x^n<=a^n<=a^N<epsilon. Threshold depends on a and epsilon, not x.

Narration: Now restrict the domain to zero through a, where a is fixed and strictly less than one. The pointwise limit is zero throughout this smaller interval. Every point x is at most a, so its nth power is at most a to the power n. That upper bound is also attained at a: it is the largest error on the whole interval.

Narration: Because a is fixed below one, its powers tend to zero. Choose a threshold for which a to that power is below epsilon. Every later power is smaller still, and every point's error is bounded by it. This threshold depends on a and epsilon, but not on x. That proves uniform convergence. The restriction supplies a single shrinking error bound; pointwise convergence on the original interval supplied only a separate promise for each fixed point.

plan.audience: Second-year mathematics students who know limits and epsilon notation
prerequisites: Powers of numbers between zero and one
plan.learningGoal: Distinguish pointwise and uniform quantifiers, prove that x^n converges pointwise but not uniformly on [0,1], and prove uniform convergence on every fixed [0,a] with 0<a<1.
plan.centralQuestion: Why does convergence at every fixed point fail to provide a common threshold on [0,1], and why does a fixed boundary a<1 provide one?
plan.keyInsight: Below one each fixed point has vanishing error, but the moving points x_n=2^(-1/n) retain error 1/2 at every index; on [0,a] all pointwise errors are bounded by the same vanishing quantity a^n.
plan.runningExample: The family f_n(x)=x^n, n>=1, first on [0,1], then restricted to [0,a] for fixed 0<a<1. The full-domain limit is 0 below 1 and 1 at 1. Use epsilon=1/4 and witness x_n=2^(-1/n). The final drawing may use a=0.8, with the proof explicitly for arbitrary fixed a.
misconceptions: The pointwise limit is zero at x=1
A large threshold at each point automatically gives one threshold for every point
A moving counterexample point contradicts pointwise convergence
The supremum error must occur at x=1 or must be attained
A visual impression of flattening proves uniform convergence
The threshold on [0,a] must be independent of a

entities.meaning: The two definitions in beat-1, with identical error conditions but pointwise N(x,epsilon) and uniform N(epsilon). Exit before the running example.

Fixed horizontal x and vertical function-value scales introduced in beat-2 and retained through beat-4. The active domain begins as [0,1]; beat-4 deliberately restricts it to [0,a] without changing scale.

The graph of x^n, BLUE, introduced in beat-2 and calculated for actual integer n in beat-3. In beat-4 the same family is restricted to [0,a]. Curve, witness and numerical readouts always use the same exponent.

GREEN target limit, introduced in beat-2: zero for x<1 and one at x=1, with explicit open/closed endpoint markers. Preserved through beat-3; restriction in beat-4 removes the excluded endpoint and leaves zero throughout [0,a].

GOLD vertical error comparison and associated error expressions. Introduced only after the limit in beat-2, distinguishes zero endpoint error from positive errors below one in beat-3, then displays the maximum a^n in beat-4. Error is always distance from the applicable pointwise limit.

YELLOW point x_n=2^(-1/n) and its corresponding point on the power graph, introduced only at beat-3 Reveal. The point approaches one from below while its height and error stay 1/2. Removed before the restricted-domain argument.
TEAL boundary x=a in beat-4; a is fixed during the argument, illustratively 0.8, with all active x bounded by a.

keyPoints: Pointwise: every x and epsilon may have their own N
Uniform: choose N for epsilon before x is specified

Reveal pointwise first and uniform second in speech order. Group each quantifier with its variable and compare the position of 'for every x' relative to 'there exists N'; display N(x,epsilon) and N(epsilon) near their own definitions. Keep the all-later-n clause present in both. No decorative graph is needed. Exit the definitions after the final spoken comparison.

scenes.purpose: Disprove uniform convergence with an explicit point for every index, while preserving pointwise convergence.
scenes.whyNow: The viewer knows the target limit and error, so can attempt the common-threshold prediction before seeing the moving witness.
keyPoints: Predict whether epsilon=1/4 has a common threshold
For each n, x_n=2^(-1/n)<1 gives error 1/2
Changing x with n is allowed when challenging uniformity
The full-domain supremum error is 1 and is not attained
scenes.visualDescription: 2D (because the argument concerns a scalar error over a scalar domain): Begin from the exact beat-2 end state. Show epsilon=1/4 as the test tolerance but keep the witness, half-height guide, answer, and near-endpoint emphasis absent throughout the five-second pause. At Reveal introduce the YELLOW moving-witness point and formula x_n=2^(-1/n), identifying its GREEN target value as zero. Show the algebra (2^(-1/n))^n=1/2 and a GOLD error segment of height 1/2. Calculate later curves and witnesses for n=32,64,128 from the same exponent: witness x changes and approaches 1, while its height stays 1/2. Preserve the filled limit point at (1,1) and zero endpoint error. After the contradiction is spoken, support the supremum claim with a fixed-n approach x -> 1 from below and e_n(x) -> 1, contrasted with e_n(1)=0; clearly label sup=1 as not attained. The witness proof, not the plot, establishes failure. Remove witness and its temporary guides before the next scene.
scenes.endsWith: Fixed axes, active power curve, full GREEN limit, and GOLD supremum error statement remain. Moving-witness marks and guides have exited, preserving the original domain for its explicit restriction next.

sourceRefs.supports: Explain why point-dependent large n does not yield one threshold for every x; include one reachable prediction and one brief pause

scenes.purpose: Prove uniform convergence on [0,a] by a single vanishing bound on every error.
scenes.whyNow: Responds directly to the near-one obstruction by restricting the domain; concludes with a complete uniform estimate.
keyPoints: Fix a<1 and restrict the domain
The restricted pointwise limit is zero everywhere
Every error is at most a^n, attained at a
a^n -> 0 gives one N for every x and every later n
scenes.visualDescription: 2D (because an ordered interval and a scalar upper bound are the mathematical evidence): Start from beat-3's actual graph. Introduce TEAL x=a, using a=0.8 for a representative drawing but keep all formulas general. Mark (a,1] as excluded before removing that curve section and the excluded GREEN endpoint; preserve the zero limit and unchanged axes on the retained domain. After the restriction is explicit, choose an illustrative current exponent such as n=4 so the maximum height is readable, then show n=8,16 with a fixed a. State this deliberate exponent change through the visible n readout; it is a comparison of family members, not a continuation of monotone time. GOLD vertical error at x=a establishes the exact maximum a^n. Display 0<=x^n<=a^n for all 0<=x<=a, then the full bound x^n<=a^n<=a^N<epsilon for n>=N. Match every height and readout to the same a,n. The shrinking maximum and inequality provide the common threshold; no control or extra pause is needed.
scenes.endsWith: The restricted BLUE graph, GREEN zero limit, fixed TEAL boundary a and GOLD bound x^n<=a^n<=a^N<epsilon for n>=N remain as the concluding proof. N depends on a and epsilon, not x.
